summary:
Chaco has no separate provincial statute on legal gender recognition, and no provincial criminalisation, enforcement series or quota-compliance finding appears in the record. A trans visitor to the province therefore stands under Argentina's national framework: Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons; Reuters reported that the decree bans gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

The National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Argentina during 2025, a rise of 62% year on year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one crime every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, 142 cases; gay men accounted for 22%, 50 cases. The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and to state legitimation of discriminatory discourse. Chaco sits under that national pattern, with no separate local record.

Institutional protection has contracted. The federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed in 2024. Trans activists interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, described a chaotic and desperate situation and said government policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020, so that the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and the United Nations described Law 26.743 as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws, though the closure of INADI removes the principal federal complaints channel.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025, with the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recording at least 227 hate crimes over the year, a record. Agencia Presentes described the figure as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
localsOnly:
Residents of Chaco face the same national legal instruments as the rest of the country: Law 26.743 governs legal gender recognition, and the February 2025 decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors restricts gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. A second decree of the same month governs the housing of transgender people in prisons.

Public-sector employment protections have narrowed in practice. Trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota were dismissed during 2024, and the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, which administered related policy, has been eliminated. The federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, removing the standard route for lodging discrimination complaints.

No provincial hate-crime series, provincial anti-discrimination statute specific to trans people, or provincial enforcement record for Chaco appears in the available sources; residents' exposure is documented only at the national level.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses Chaco specifically. Whether the province operates its own anti-discrimination body, hate-crime reporting channel or public-sector trans employment scheme after the federal changes is unresolved and not sourced here.

Unresolved: whether the February 2025 decrees have been reviewed by the courts following the announced intention to seek judicial intervention, and whether any provincial court in Chaco has applied or declined the travesticidio aggravating circumstance.

Not sourced: entry, visa and document-screening practice for trans travellers at Argentine border points, access to gender-affirming care in Chaco's public health facilities, and the availability of gender-neutral identification markers or bathroom and facility rules at provincial level. Outright International's negative assessment of civil-society organisation registration is recorded without the underlying criteria.
